anchors.fact: Ciro Capozzi (1855–1938), a sea captain's son from the Bay of Naples, head bartender of a small American bar facing the Monte Carlo casino from about 1885; his own bar from 1888 (pdf 460–461). F1, F2, F5
anchors.meaning: A barman, behind the bar, not a host on a stage. "About 1885", never a bare year.

anchors.fact: Where other European bars poured fantasies with names like "Heaps of Comfort", he served drinks "far simpler", and brought Europe the Manhattan (pdf 460). F4
anchors.meaning: Nothing showy: the hold was the person and the care, not the trick.

anchors.fact: His guests were "very strongly English", among them the prince of Wales, who would show him cocktails he had learned; with him and the newspaper owner James Gordon Bennett as regulars, the best of the season's society followed (pdf 461). Habitual, undated, no drink named. **Counterweight:** the prince already liked American drinks when most of his circle didn't (pdf 491), so never "won him over". F6, F7
anchors.meaning: The most watched man in the room brought something of his own to the bar. Around this guest, people feel free to offer something. Any "relaxed" or "at home" is "I like to think".

anchors.fact: Oxford: "charm, skill, and hospitality" gave him the leverage to move the culture; to say he made the cocktail fashionable in Europe "might be an exaggeration", "but it would not be much of one" (pdf 462). F12
anchors.meaning: The warmth worked, and it changed what a whole society drank. Keep the hedge whenever the claim is made. Paraphrase in the reading; "charm" is never praise of the guest.

anchors.fact: His wife Clotilde ran the till and his brother Salvatore the bar; it "ran smoothly" until 1911 (pdf 461). F8
anchors.meaning: Optional. The room rested on him, but others held it too.

anchors.fact: In 1911 he sold to London investors and retired to his villa nearby, living quietly for another twenty-seven years (pdf 461). F9
anchors.kind: the stepping away (not in reading v2)
anchors.meaning: He stopped. The question the guest never asks, answered once in the record.

anchors.fact: The new owners kept "the same formula" and opened in Paris in 1912, an instant success (pdf 461); the Monte Carlo house itself ran until "the immediate postwar years" (pdf 462), some three decades after he left (our arithmetic; the war is read from context). F10, F11
anchors.kind: what kept going (not in reading v2)
anchors.meaning: They kept coming after he'd gone. Never say he watched, or that it was the same without him; never "after him" from Oxford's kings sentence (C2).

anchors.fact: (Reading v2: ours is rye, sweet vermouth, bitters; no page says what Ciro's Manhattan was made with, so the recipe is said as mine, audit v2 H2.) The Manhattan had reached Monte Carlo by the end of the 1880s (pdf 1224); he was introducing it to Europe (pdf 460). F4, F16
anchors.meaning: Why a Manhattan, plain. Tomás owns the recipe; never "his recipe" for our riff.

anchors.fact: His own Cocktail, 1898: bitters, a half barspoon of orange curaçao, a little rich syrup, genever, cognac or American whiskey, stirred, up, lemon twist (pdf 491–492, Wondrich's measures). F15
anchors.meaning: Optional source for the spark or the twist: something from his own glass. Tomás's call.

anchors.fact: The prince had a cocktail of his own: a London paper of July 1887 describes "the drink the prince concocted" (Oxford PRINCE OF WALES, pdf 1562), and a 1901 book says he "is credited with having composed" it (*Imbibe!* pdf 231). Rye, a small piece of pineapple, Angostura, lemon peel, a little maraschino and champagne, sugar. Our glass takes only the pineapple. F17
anchors.meaning: What the guest brought to the bar, in the glass. **Signpost the link:** the page says he showed Ciro "cocktails he had learned" (pdf 461), never which, so "I like to think this one was among them". Never "his recipe" or "the prince's cocktail" for ours. In guest text, say "a cocktail of his own" with its channel ("as a London paper had it in 1887", one paper, the *Evening Telegraph*; or "it was credited to him"); never cite the 1901 book's title (a royal word), and don't name the drink by its title (the prince appears once). F18

anchors.fact: In 1887 pineapple was "extraordinarily costly", and Oxford reads the prince's drink as "conspicuous consumption" (pdf 1562). Wondrich files it as a variation on the Improved Whiskey Cocktail (*Imbibe!* pdf 230). F17, F19
anchors.meaning: The pineapple was the showy part of *his* glass, so never call it humble or modest. In ours it's hidden at the rim: that's our change, said as ours. Never "Improved" in our lineage (*Beside the First*).

cocktail.closingLine: Strain the pineapple out. It's still there at the rim. So are you, even when you're not trying.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Put the pineapple and the syrup in a mixing glass or jar. Press the pineapple with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin until its juice runs.
Add the rye, the vermouth and the bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Empty the cocktail glass. Strain the drink into it through a small tea strainer, so no pineapple gets through.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Up Close

recipe.note: cut from near the base, where it's sweetest; no bigger, or the drink turns sharp
2 parts sugar to 1 part water, stirred until clear
any straight rye, 40% or stronger; the numbers were run on 50%
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: People remember how you made them feel because you remember who they are.

reading.epigraph: A Monte Carlo barman kept his Manhattans plain. This one borrows from a regular's cocktail.
whoYouAre: Someone comes back after a year away, and you ask about the interview they were dreading. You remember their sister's name. You stay with them a second longer than they expect. They go home feeling remembered.

You know exactly what your attention does, and you give it on purpose, because a lot holds together when you do. People who watch from further off call it charm, and sometimes mean it as a warning. They've got it backwards: it works because you mean it. You hardly mention what it costs, or the question underneath: if I stopped, would they still come? The fear is the evening it doesn't land, when someone looks past you and everything quietly drifts. And this is what your attention gives: people leave feeling they were the one who mattered, and sure enough to offer something of their own. On an ordinary evening, nobody expects to be given that.
yours: In about 1885, a sea captain's son from near Naples was made head bartender of a small bar facing the casino in Monte Carlo. Ciro Capozzi had actually tended bar in America, and where other bars poured inventions called things like Flip Flaps, he served far simpler drinks, the Manhattan among them.

His own bar opened in 1888, just off the casino square, and among its regulars was the Prince of Wales, who would show him cocktails he had learned. He liked American drinks already, so Ciro never had to win him over. He kept coming back, with what he knew. I like to think Ciro treasured that: the most watched man in Monte Carlo, at ease enough to teach the barman.

People look for the trick in you, and there isn't one. The plainness is the point: someone paying real attention, and meaning it. And the best of it was never that people are charmed. It's what they bring you once they feel seen. Anyone can be charming for an evening. You remember, you return to it, and so people offer you their best.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Manhattan, the renowned classic Ciro was pouring in Monte Carlo. Mine is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters, stirred until ice-cold, then brightened with lemon peel. To it I've added a small square of fresh pineapple, from a cocktail of that regular's own, as a London paper had it in 1887. I like to think his own was among the ones he showed Ciro. Back then a pineapple was hugely expensive, and his drink showed it off. In this glass it goes quiet: pressed with a touch of syrup, then strained out again, as a nod to what a regular brings to the bar. It still looks like a plain Manhattan. You only find the pineapple up close.

Soon, for once, don't be "on". Let someone else carry the conversation, and let them show you something they've learned. Then you'll see whether they'd still come, and I hope the answer surprises you, in the best way.
